entry.title: Week 2 in one page: Multi-Stream Attention

link.title: Week 2 in one page: Multi-Stream Attention

entry.content:
The Paper’s Main Points

The paper discusses residual connections in LLMs, it builds upon and improves a line of literature that has seeked to replace the standard skip connection. The standard skip connection has a major flaw — information dilution, all previous layer representations are compressed into a single vector. Previous works like mHC and AttnRes have improved on this by suggesting an attention-like mechanism for selectively and dynamically attending to previous layer representations. Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR) wishes to extend this into a multi-head(stream) attention, the challenge presented is doing so without additional linear projections or presistent memory. The authours solve this using causal convolutions along the sequence dimension, expanding previous layer hidden states into multiple representations (streams), for which they apply depth-wise attention like in AttnRes then fuse represntations back into a single vector like in mHC.

What we made

✍️ Writing: clearing up jurgon and notations

Writing this week focused on clarity. Many in class felt the paper requires a strong background that wasn’t clearly presented (expressed in the main points post); the abstract rewrite focused on fixing this and making the paper more accessible. The methods section rewrite improved clarity by replacing the difficult-to-follow formal notation with a simple table that summarizes the method. Another abstract rewrite chose to highlight the most compelling result (1.58x iso-loss compute speedup) earlier in the abstract, where reader attention is at its peak.

🧠 Learning: strengthening our base

Explaing HC and mHC post provides an in-depth overview of a key advancement in the modern residual connections lien of work. It walks the reader through one of the more mathematically complex solutions in this field, explaining the rational behind it and providing clear examples — a must-read for anyone looking to dive deeper into this research area. What are these evals anyway? is a high-level and comprehensive review of LLM evaluations, including the different categories of evaluations, their meaning, and even some very helpful examples from popular evals, very valuable information for approaching any paper across the LLMs domain and trying to decide what “being better” actually means.

📊 Visualization: choose the explanation that clicks

Some of this week`s visualizations focused on conveying the paper’s main mechanism and which hidden states contribute to the residual connection of each layer, suggesting an alternative to the paper’s figure2 and designing an interactive interface that allows playing with diffrent configurations. Another suggestion was A better Figure 1, tweaking its presentation to suggest a better first impression. Finally, A Better Figure 1(c) suggests a revisualization of the evaluation comparision results, adding the dynamics of these results across scales.

🔬 Research: the missing control

The author background helps us understand the paper is part of the authors’ current work towards perfecting residual connections (More recent work xHC) as part of their overall research theme of improving LLM pretraining by optimizing aspects of the architecture design. The literature review provides context that came up again and again in class as essential for understanding this paper.

This week’s critiques (1, 2, 3, 4) while mostly positive emphsizing the impressive empirical gains and the succesfull effort to minimize the cost they come at, all boil down to the same question: is the mechanism nessecary or are the gains coming from somewhere else? Critique 1 praised the w/o convolution control in this context while the other critiques mentioned “Canon layers” that improve performance via a causal convolution before attention and before the MLP alone (Allen-Zhu, 2025), suggesting the authors conflated the local context bias from the convolutions with their multihead attention. Critique 4 provides a suggestion for a control to test this theory: “AttnRes plus a single causal convolution on the sources, one head. Add Vanilla plus Canon-A/C. If these match MSAR, the contribution is token mixing.”

The proposed follow-up tests an asymmetric design using multi-stream retrieval for Attention sublayers and standard residual connectionss for the subsequent MLPs. The rational lies within the depth-wise attention maps visualizations from the paper appendix which show MLPs primarily rely on the immediate preceding sublayer anyway, this approach could drastically cut memory I/O overhead without sacrificing performance.

🔭 Scouting: depth scaling and more

The scouting posts (1, 2, 3) presented a few complementary directions as well as unrelated interesting developments. Recurrent Looped Transformer and Skip a Layer or Loop It? Learning Program-of-Layers in LLMs presented in scouting posts 1 and 2 both tackle dynamic scaling of LLM depth, perhaps suggesting an alternative solution to the residual dilution problem when increasing depth.

📣 Communication: from the article to a feed

The LinkedIn post presents the rationale for adapting a familiar idea like multi-head attention to AttnRes. There is also a video explainer.

entry.title: Critique of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR)
entry.content:
Summary of the claims

MSAR targets depth-wise information dilution: the standard residual connection (h_{l+1} = h_l + f_l(h_l)) compresses every prior computation into one growing sum with fixed unit weights, so early-layer features get diluted and later layers struggle to retrieve them. The paper builds directly on Attention Residuals (AttnRes), which replaces the residual sum with a content-dependent softmax retrieval over earlier layer outputs — “single-head attention along the depth axis.”

The central claim is that this can be generalized to multi-head depth attention at near-zero cost. The authors first argue that the obvious routes fail: channel-splitting the hidden state breaks the integrity of the value vector (and empirically degrades AttnRes), and deriving candidate streams via H^post-style write-back yields near-identical keys after normalization (no head diversity). Their solution draws diversity from the sequence axis instead: cheap multi-scale causal depthwise convolutions expand each single-stream source into m full-dimensional “views” (kernels {4,8,12}, m=4), each view runs its own depth attention with its own learned pseudo-query, and the retrieved streams are fused with a lightweight mHC-style H^pre scalar mixer. Block MSAR stores only single-stream block summaries and expands them on demand, keeping persistent storage/communication at O(Nd) (matching AttnRes), with fused-kernel expansion and two-phase computation holding overhead to +0.5% FLOPs / +0.3% activated params.

Empirically they claim: (1) lowest final training loss at 18B (1.750 vs Vanilla 1.799, mHC 1.776, AttnRes 1.769); (2) wins on all 12 downstream benchmarks at both 18B and 28B MoE scale (avg +8.2/+7.8 over Vanilla, +3.9/+3.0 over AttnRes); (3) an iso-loss compute speedup of 1.58× over Vanilla vs 1.35× (AttnRes) and 1.30× (mHC); and (4) ablations showing the convolutional source diversity — not query diversity or a naive AttnRes+mHC sum — is what drives the gain.

Strengths

  • Well-motivated and well-framed. The time–depth duality framing is intuitive, and the paper explicitly dissects why the naive multi-head routes fail before proposing its own — a genuine scientific argument rather than a “we tried X and it worked” report.
  • Strong cost/benefit. A 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup for +0.5% FLOPs is a meaningful architectural result, and it dominates two already-strong baselines rather than just beating a vanilla strawman.
  • Consistency over cherry-picking. It wins all 12 benchmarks at both model scales and improves the entire fitted scaling-law curve across four scales — the result is systemic, not a single lucky number.
  • Ablations isolate the mechanism. The w/o Conv row (identical streams, independent queries → 1.847 to 1.862) shows source diversity matters more than query diversity, and the AttnRes + mHC combo (1.861) rules out “it’s just adding two existing tricks.” The learned-attention visualizations (App. D) confirm streams genuinely specialize.
  • Systems-aware. O(Nd) storage, fused expansion kernels, two-phase computation, and cross-stage caching are designed for real frontier-scale pre-training, and the baselines (mHC, AttnRes) are the actual state of practice (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3).

Weaknesses

  • Pre-training metrics only. All results are training loss + few-shot downstream accuracy. There is no instruction-tuning / RLHF / long-context evaluation, so it’s unknown whether the gains survive post-training — the thing practitioners actually care about.
  • No variance reported. Single runs, no seeds or error bars. Several per-benchmark margins (e.g. HumanEval +0.6, MATH +0.8 at 28B) are plausibly within run-to-run noise.
  • FLOPs ≠ wall-clock. The headline speedup is compute-normalized, but MSAR adds real memory traffic over AttnRes (~21.5d vs 5.5d per sublayer, Table 6) from writing/reading the m retrieved streams for H^pre aggregation. No throughput/latency numbers are given, so the practical speedup is unverified.
  • Hand-picked design choices. Kernel sizes {4,8,12} are chosen, not learned or searched, with little intuition for why these scales or sensitivity analysis around them.
  • Inference underexplored. The analysis centers on training/prefill; decode-time cost and KV-cache / long-context interactions are largely undiscussed.
  • Comparison is not fully independent. The key baselines (AttnRes, xHC) come from the same research group, and this is a very recent, non-peer-reviewed preprint.

How it could have been improved

  • Add post-training evaluation (SFT + a chat/agentic benchmark) to show the pre-training gain transfers to deployed quality.
  • Report multiple seeds / confidence intervals, at minimum on the 10B ablation model, so small per-benchmark deltas are interpretable.
  • Provide a wall-clock throughput and peak-memory table (tokens/sec, activation memory) next to FLOPs — the real question is time-to-loss on hardware, where the extra memory traffic could matter.
  • Learn or search m and the kernel sizes (or show robustness to them), e.g. letting deeper layers use wider receptive fields.
  • Push to larger scale — the baselines live at trillion-param scale, and architectural gaps sometimes shrink with scale, so demonstrating the 1.58× persists further out would strengthen the claim.
  • Analyze inference / long-context behavior and interaction with KV-cache compression.

Verdict

Would I accept it? Yes. The idea is novel and clearly motivated, the empirical case is strong and consistent against the right baselines, and the ablations do real work isolating the mechanism. The weaknesses are about completeness (post-training, variance, wall-clock) rather than the core claim being unconvincing — these are revision requests, not grounds for rejection.

Is the direction worth pursuing? Yes, conditionally. The method is cheap to implement and the payoff compounds over a full pre-training budget, so it’s worth integrating and re-validating. But pursue it with eyes open: before betting a frontier run on it, confirm that (1) the FLOPs win translates to wall-clock on real hardware despite the added memory traffic, and (2) it survives post-training and holds at larger scale. The open question is not “does it work?” — the loss and benchmark evidence are convincing — but “does the measured efficiency gain translate to practice?”
entry.summary: A clever, low-cost multi-head generalization of depth-wise residual retrieval with strong, consistent pre-training gains — but the win is shown only in FLOPs and pre-training loss, not wall-clock or post-training.

entry.title: Key Points Multi Stream Attention Residuals

link.title: Key Points Multi Stream Attention Residuals

entry.content:
title: “Multi-Head Depth Attention Is Not Just Multiple Queries” description: “What MSAR really adds to AttnRes, and how the paper could make it clearer.”paper: multi-stream-attention-residuals role: writing task: key-points by: Reuvenspitz —

I think the main challenge in reading this paper is understanding what exactly MSAR adds to previous residual methods. The paper has several design choices, and I think it would be easier to follow if the motivation for each one was explained separately.

1. From residual connections to multi-head depth attention

In standard residual connections, each layer adds its output to the accumulated hidden state, with a fixed weight of 1.

AttnRes changes this by using softmax attention to decide how much information to retrieve from previous layers, instead of simply adding their outputs.

MSAR extends this idea to multiple depth-attention heads, inspired by multi-head attention in regular Transformers.

But this brings us to an important question: what exactly does it mean to have multiple heads over depth?

2. Multi-head depth attention is not just multiple queries

This is the point I think deserves more attention in the paper.

The most straightforward idea would be to use different queries for different heads. Each head could then focus on different previous layers.

But if all heads use the same source vectors, and we combine their outputs with scalar weights, the final result is still a weighted sum of the original sources. The weights may be computed in a more complicated way, but we are still combining the same vectors.

MSAR goes one step further by giving each head a different representation of the sources themselves.

The authors do this using causal depthwise convolutions. One stream keeps the original source, while the others combine information from the current and previous tokens using different window sizes.

So there are two operations on different axes: convolution across tokens creates different source representations, and attention across layers decides which historical sources to retrieve.

The retrieved streams are then combined using learned, input-dependent weights.

I think this separation between different attention distributions and different source representations is important for understanding the contribution.

3. The efficiency and experimental results are also part of the contribution

A natural concern is that multiple streams could require much more memory. MSAR addresses this by storing only single-stream sources. The additional streams are computed from these sources when depth attention needs them, rather than being stored permanently.

Like AttnRes, it also supports block summaries instead of storing every layer output separately. This allows Block MSAR to match Block AttnRes in persistent source storage and pipeline communication costs.

The experimental results support the design. MSAR outperforms Vanilla residual connections, mHC, and AttnRes on all 12 benchmarks at both the 18B and 28B model scales. The scaling-law experiments also report a 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup over Vanilla, compared to 1.35× for AttnRes.

I think one particularly important result is the ablation without convolution. On a 10B model, using four queries over identical sources gives a loss of 1.862, compared to 1.867 for AttnRes. With convolution, MSAR reaches 1.847.

This helps show that the improvement is not simply from adding more queries. The convolutional source expansion is an important part of the method.

What I would change in the presentation

I would make the steps from AttnRes to MSAR clearer before introducing the equations in Section 3.2:

  1. First, explain what we gain from having multiple depth-attention heads.
  2. Then explain why using different queries over the same sources is limited, and why the authors also want different source representations.
  3. Finally, explain why convolution is used to create these representations efficiently.

I would also make the two axes more visible in Figure 2. The figure shows the causal convolutions, but not how they combine information from different token positions. I think showing this would help readers understand the connection between the two axes.

I would also mention the result without convolution (1.862 vs. 1.847) right after the method, not only in Table 2, because it is the clearest evidence that the source expansion matters.

For me, this would make it easier to understand not only how MSAR works, but also why the authors chose this architecture.

entry.title: MSAR paper on LinkedIn
entry.content:
LinkedIn

Turns out that familiar ideas like multi-head attention can still yield substantial gains when applied along a different axis. Residual connections help deep networks train by letting information and gradients flow directly across layers. But as successive layer outputs accumulate in a single residual stream, earlier features can become diluted and harder for later layers to access selectively.

Attention Residuals addresses this by letting layers attend directly to earlier representations. A new paper, Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), extends that approach to multiple streams: different heads retrieve representations from earlier layers through different views of the sequence context.

In scaling-law experiments, the authors report a 1.58× compute advantage over standard residual connections at the same loss, compared with 1.35× for Attention Residuals and 1.30× for manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections.

A nice example of how a well-established idea can yield gains in new applications.

Paper: https://lnkd.in/damRha3s

Sunan Zou

Posted at: https://lnkd.in/p/dUrd6Ykm

entry.title: Visualizing Core ideas
entry.content:
Core idea

We are aware of two scaling axes that can be used to achieve stronger inteligence from models:

  1. Bigger models - Use more data to train more parameters.
  2. Chain-of-thought - Use test time compute by training the model to output more tokens.

The paper’s core idea is to allow for test time compute, but by using latent space reasoning instead of more output tokens. The architecture to allow it is the recurrent depth architecture.

The figure

How to read it

  • A new scaling axis A test time compute scaling axis that isn’t dependant on the number of output tokens, or on training data.
  • Recurrent depth architecture An architecture to allow the new test time compute scaling axis.

Results (not in the figure). One nested run uses 36% less training compute than three independent runs, and speculative decoding is 26% faster than with an independently trained pair (greedy, draft length 6). Accuracy is within 0.5 average points of token-matched baselines, which use 57% more compute.

Caveats. The 3.2B vs. 5.2B count leaves out the LM heads of the two smaller exits (about 0.16B), and part of the decoding speedup comes from a larger batch fitting in memory (102 vs. 64).
entry.summary: One figure showing how three separate models become one nested model, how the blocks connect, and how the smaller models learn from the largest.

entry.title: Key points of Multi Stream Attention

link.title: Key points of Multi Stream Attention

entry.content:
The general rule

Using technical jargon might make your abstract shorter - but it’ll take twice as long to read. Start the paper (abstract, intro) giving the readers some context on the problem you are trying to solve and on what is the state of solutions today, and USE VISUALIZATIONS.

Reading the abstract, a reader with no sufficient context on the innovations in the field (like myself) will be lost quickly (after being attacked by “content-dependent retrieval” and “single-stream softmax attention” in the first sentence, and the first architecture figure in page 7).

After doing some catching up, I think the main points of the paper could be described like so:

1. Residual streams could be upgraded to be non-uniform with attention

This is not a new contribution by the paper, but it is the main important context I was missing, and it’s one of the more interesting things I learned going over this paper. The credit for this idea (as far as I could tell) goes to Attention Residuals (AttnRes) (Kimi Team, 2026), which builds on earlier ways of letting a layer read all previous layers directly (Huang et al., 2017; Pagliardini et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025).

2. Attention over both depth AND tokens (/time)

A previous architecture - AttnRes - used attention on the residual stream of this same token. In this paper they expand this to both look across the different network layers as well as across each layer’s reaction to the previous tokens (here - up to 12 previous tokens). Another expansion of this idea is the use of multi-headed attention here. In this paper they use the convolution over the token history as the way to combine these. Here as well the idea isn’t novel (Mixture-of-Depths Attention attends over both tokens and earlier layers (Zhu et al., 2026), and short convolutions over previous tokens appear in Primer and Canon layers (So et al., 2021; Allen-Zhu, 2025)), but the use of convolutions for inter-token mixing in the depth attention is new as far as I could tell.

3. We made it work properly on production-sized models

Maybe the biggest contribution of the paper, in my view, is showing how they combined the first two points and using clever parametrization and caching they made it work on a large scale model, showing improvements over both vanilla architecture and previous attempts that scale to large models (not the biggest, but 18B and 28B are respectable models and not a model organism (even though this is the MoE total parameter count, not active)). Caveat that should be stated here - this is a properly sized model but the compute budget for training is much much smaller than that of a “proper” production size LLM.

How they could have done better

Maybe the paper isn’t aimed at outsiders, but as one trying to read it - bringing me “up to speed” wouldn’t have taken more than a few lines, written in simple english, and creating a more in depth view of their architectural suggestion (i.e figure 2, with a bit more focus on the architectural changes and most importantly - much earlier in the paper). Additionally, I thing the framing of attention over both depth (of the network) and over previous tokens jointly is more helpful (at least to me).

The main contribution of this paper are it’s results, which the paper presents in a very forward manner (abstract, first figure). They would be easier to understand given the context of the architectural changes.
entry.summary: They had a point, I'm sure it's buried in here somewhere.

entry.title: Rewriting the abstract of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

link.title: Rewriting the abstract of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract presents the technical details quite densely, making it difficult to immediately understand the motivation behind the method and what distinguishes it from previous approaches. I reorganized it to first introduce the problem, then explain the limitation of AttnRes and present MSAR as the proposed solution. I also improved the flow between the methodology, efficiency advantages, and experimental results.

Before and after

Before Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth, which can be viewed as single-stream softmax attention along the depth axis. Inspired by the success of multi-head attention along the sequence axis, we introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), an extension of AttnRes that generalizes this mechanism to multi-head depth attention, yielding substantial performance gains with minimal additional overhead. MSAR draws stream diversity from sequence context through multi-scale causal convolutions, allowing different heads to retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views while preserving the integrity of the hidden representation. The retrieved streams are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to generate the single-stream layer input. By retaining single-stream sources and expanding them on demand, MSAR supports multi-stream computation without requiring persistent multi-stream storage or communication. Across all 12 downstream benchmarks at the 18B and 28B MoE scales, MSAR consistently outperforms prior residual variants, including standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes. Scaling-law experiments yield an iso-loss compute speedup of 1.58× over the standard residual baseline, compared with 1.35× for AttnRes and 1.30× for mHC. These results make MSAR a promising residual architecture for large-scale pre-training.
After Deep Transformer models can struggle to effectively retrieve information from earlier layers, limiting the benefits of increasing network depth. Attention Residuals (AttnRes) address this challenge by using attention to retrieve information from previous layers, but rely on a single attention stream. We introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), which extends this approach by enabling multiple attention streams to independently retrieve information from previous layers. To create diverse streams without reducing the dimensionality of hidden representations, MSAR uses multi-scale causal convolutions that capture different ranges of sequence context. Each stream performs its own attention over previous layers, and the retrieved representations are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to produce a single input for the next layer. Furthermore, MSAR generates additional streams only when needed, avoiding the need to store or communicate multiple persistent representations. Experiments at the 18B and 28B MoE scales demonstrate that MSAR consistently outperforms standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes across all 12 downstream benchmarks. Scaling-law experiments further show a 1.58× compute speedup over standard residual connections at equivalent training loss, compared with 1.35× for AttnRes and 1.30× for mHC. These results demonstrate that MSAR can improve the efficiency and performance of large-scale Transformer pre-training.

The general rule

Introduce the problem before describing the proposed method. Explain the limitations of existing approaches to establish why a new method is needed, then present the main contribution and how it addresses those limitations. Finally, highlight the most important experimental results. An abstract should communicate the motivation, novelty, and significance of a paper in a logical order without overwhelming readers with technical details.
entry.summary: A new approach to Transformer residual connections that improves performance while reducing the computational cost of deep learning.

entry.title: Critique of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals -“
entry.content:
Summary of the claims

The paper upgrades single-stream depth attention (AttnRes) into multi-head depth attention. It creates multiple streams from earlier layers by running short causal convolutions across neighboring tokens, lets each stream attend over depth independently, and mixes them back into a single layer input.

Strengths

MSAR generalizes single-stream depth attention into a multi-head retrieval mechanism, allowing layers to query earlier blocks through multiple parallel attention distributions and achieving strong scaling with minimal overhead.

Weaknesses

MSAR attributes its gains to multi-head depth attention, using 1D depthwise causal convolutions (K in {4, 8, 12}) to generate diverse source streams from neighboring tokens. However, injecting short causal convolutions into the residual path introduces explicit local sequence mixing before every Attention and MLP/MoE sublayer—an inductive bias already known to independently improve language modeling in architectures like Mamba and hybrid Transformers. In Table 2, removing the convolutions while keeping 4 query heads (w/o Conv) degrades Pile loss, nearly reverting to single-stream AttnRes. The authors interpret this drop as proof that depth-attention heads need source diversity, but it is equally consistent with the convolutions themselves doing the heavy lifting via local token mixing while the multiple depth queries add very little.

Verdict

Accept, as the empirical gains on 18B and 28B MoE models are strong, but the paper needs a control experiment adding the same convolutions to a single-stream baseline to verify that the gains actually come from multi-head depth routing rather than local token mixing.
entry.summary: One sentence summary of your take.

entry.title: Critique of of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

link.title: Critique of of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

entry.content:
Summary of the claims

The paper introduces MSAR, a new residual architecture that extends AttnRes by using multiple streams with different contextual views. The authors show improvements in training loss and downstream performance over Vanilla, mHC, and AttnRes, with relatively small computational overhead.

Strengths

Results are strong across both model scales and all 12 benchmark : MSAR improves over all three baselines on all 12 downstream benchmarks at both 18B and 28B model scales.

The paper considers practical efficiency, not just performance : adds only 0.3% activated parameters and 0.5% training FLOPs relative to Vanilla.

Weaknesses

It is not fully clear which component is responsible for the gains : The paper doesn’t show whether the gains come from multi-head depth attention or from the added convolutions and other architectural changes.

Figure placement: The main figure explaining the method appears only on page 7, rather than near the beginning of the paper.

How it could have been improved

Better isolate the contribution of multi-head depth attention from the convolutions.

Verdict

I would lean toward weak accept. The results are strong and the idea is interesting, especially given the small reported overhead. However, I would like to see more experiments explaining why MSAR works and whether the gains generalize beyond the tested models.
entry.summary: An interesting and efficient architecture with strong results, but its individual contributions could be better isolated.

entry.title: Follow-ups on Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
entry.content:
Follow-ups worth doing

Asymmetric Multi-Stream Residuals Across Sublayer Types

  • The Question: Can we significantly reduce the memory access bottleneck of MSAR by deploying multi-stream retrieval ($m=4$) exclusively before Attention sublayers, while keeping standard single-stream residuals before MLP sublayers?

  • The Experiment:
    1. Train a 10B MoE model using the architecture and Pile training budget described in Table 2 and in Table 3 (Appendix A).
    2. Evaluate four configurations under identical training tokens and compute budgets:
      • Full MSAR (Default): $m=4$ streams applied to both Attention and MLP sublayers.
      • Asymmetric MSAR: $m=4$ streams prior to Attention sublayers; MLP sublayers bypass multi-stream expansion and the $\mathcal{H}^{Pre}$ mixer entirely, relying on standard single-stream residual connections.
      • Standard Baselines: Vanilla residuals and Block AttnRes as reference baselines.
    3. Measure the final pre-training loss on Pile, downstream benchmark scores, and wall-clock training throughput (tokens/sec) alongside memory I/O cost.
    4. Visualize the learned Pre-Attn depth-attention weights (replicating Figure 4) to verify that restricting MLP sublayers to a single stream does not degrade the cross-depth diversity of Attention sublayers.
  • Why it’s worth someone’s time: The authors identify memory access cost as the primary operational overhead of MSAR: Table 6 shows that forward-pass memory I/O reaches $21.5d$ per token per sublayer for Block MSAR, compared to only $5.5d$ for AttnRes and $3d$ for Vanilla. However, the attention weight visualizations in Section D (Figure 4) reveal a striking contrast: Pre-Attention reads retrieve broadly across historical blocks and utilize diverse streams, whereas Pre-MLP reads focus almost entirely on the local diagonal (the immediate preceding sublayer). Allocating $m=4$ full retrieval streams to MLP sublayers incurs heavy memory traffic for operations that show little cross-depth diversity. An asymmetric design directly eliminates this inefficiency, potentially preserving MSAR’s performance gains while drastically cutting memory bandwidth overhead.
entry.summary: Cutting memory bandwidth overhead via asymmetric residual stream allocation between Attention and MLP sublayers.
